title: Expectations
text: This section outlines our expectations for anyone who is a member of the lab group. Familiarizing yourself with these expectations is essential for anyone joining the group; if you do not feel that you can abide by or tolerate these expectations, our group may not be a good fit for you.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Expectations
text: There are many roles within any research group, and each carries a different set of responsibilities and expectations. We want the lab group to be a healthy, fun, and productive place where we can make scientific progress.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Expectations
text:
Everyone

Be Present: Everyone should maintain a presence in the lab.
Work Professionally: Academia provides a lot of freedom and flexibility, but you should treat this job as you would any other.
Do Work You Are Proud Of: We work on issues of societal relevance, and we are in academia to learn things and be creative. If you aren’t proud of your work or you find yourself working on things that you don’t find interesting or you don’t think others will care about, let Vivek know as soon as possible.
Take Time Off: Take appropriate time off from work each day and each week, and take vacation to recharge.
Treat Others With Respect: Beyond our (the university’s and this group’s) policies on harassment, we expect that you will treat every other member of the lab, as well as everyone else, with respect. We want to create an environment where everybody, regardless of background and personality, feels comfortable and valued. Discussions should always be constructive.
Be Collaborative: This is likely to be a research group where everyone has different, but complementary, backgrounds, interests, and skills. Collaborations among group members is strongly encouraged. One of the goals of our regular lab meetings is to allow group members to ask questions, share where they might be stuck, and potentially get insights and advice from other members. You should never view any of your fellow group members as competition. All members of the group are expected to try to help if another member is stuck or otherwise needs advice.
Scientific Integrity: It is never okay to commit scientific misconduct. Even the slightest fudging of results to make them look better is unacceptable. We are here to gain scientific insights, not just publish papers, and nuanced and null results are still important findings. Our work will be completely reproducible and open. We have a zero-tolerance policy towards fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism. Our expectations for AI tools follow from this: you are responsible for everything in your analysis and your manuscript, including parts a tool helped produce. Make sure you familiarize yourself with the relevant portions of Cornell’s policies on responsible conduct of research and alert Vivek if you are concerned about any research practices you observe. If Vivek is the cause of your concern or you would rather he not know of your complaint, you can use a university-wide contact instead.
Open and Accessible Research Products: As a lab, we are committed to the principles of open and transparent science. We want our peers and the public to be able to reproduce, improve upon, and critique our work. Moreover, as our work is funded by public institutions, our research products should be thought of as public property. More details on our approach to openness are provided elsewhere, but all group members will make their models, data, and code publicly available and easily accessible.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Expectations
text:
Principal Investigator
Vivek has a variety of responsibilities as the PI, in addition to those outlined above.

Build a diverse, inclusive, and equitable environment: While every member of the research group is expected to contribute to a positive and inclusive environment, it is ultimately Vivek’s responsibility to manage the social dynamic of the group.
Provide the research environment: Our group’s work is primarily computational. Providing and managing hardware and software resources to facilitate the group’s research is Vivek’s job.
Obtain funding: It is Vivek’s responsibility to obtain funding for research equipment, personnel, and other costs such as travel and publication fees. One of the Vivek’s key goals is to never have to let someone go for lack of funding.
Provide material support: You are never expected to spend your personal finances on anything related to research. Coordinate any upcoming expenses with Vivek and he will identify grant support for payment or reimbursement.
Provide moral support: Academic life can be stressful, whether it’s classwork, research, the paper submission process, or job searches. Vivek is always here to listen and provide advice (see also Health and Wellness).
Provide mentoring: One of Vivek’s core jobs is to help junior researchers in the group mature into independent scientists. This mentoring role can continue, to the degree you wish, beyond your departure from the research group.






NotePlease Ask to See Documents!





As part of the mentoring process, please feel free to request access to grant proposals or other relevant documents that Vivek is working on or has completed. Vivek can discuss these with you as well.



Provide feedback: Vivek will provide feedback on all aspects of research through ongoing conversations with you. These include research hypotheses, figure designs, identification of appropriate methods, code development, data management, and paper writing. If relevant, he will also provide feedback on course selection, long-term strategy, and career goals. If Vivek is not well-suited to provide feedback on a particular topic, he will connect you with someone who is better suited.






NoteBe Mindful About Time Constraints





As a faculty member, Vivek has many demands on his time, including teaching and departmental and professional service. While Vivek will manage his time so that he can meet the listed expectations, he may not be able to provide immediate feedback during particularly busy periods. You will be given notice when this is the case as well as a rough timeline for when you can expect feedback.



Write recommendations: Recommendation letters are required for career moves. Vivek will write an honest recommendation letter for you at any point. If you need a recommendation letter, please give Vivek any required information with a few weeks’ advance notice. If you have been away from the group for some time, Vivek may ask you for some additional information to help write the letter.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Expectations
text:
Postdocs
Postdocs should be focused on transitioning into independent researchers. This does not mean working without guidance or supervision, but rather developing the ability to formulate and pursue independent lines of research.

Develop your own line of research: As a postdoc, you should develop the ability to independently identify interesting questions and develop a research plan to address them. Vivek will help guide you through this process and provide feedback.
Publish and present research: Your primarily role as a postdoc is to produce research. You will be given a large degree of autonomy when it comes to writing manuscript for publication and developing presentations for seminars or conferences.
Co-develop group research: Postdocs will bring their own expertise to the group, and are likely to have different perspectives on problems and methods than Vivek. You should take an active role in discussing parts of the research group agenda with Vivek and in meetings so that your insights can be incorporated into the group’s research portfolio.
Mentor students: As a leader in the research group, a postdoc will at some point be expected to help mentor graduate and undergraduate students in the group. This mentoring will likely be primarily focused on research, but you may have useful perspectives on work-life balance and classwork as well, and sharing these are strongly encouraged.
Develop a career plan: Postdocs have a lot of autonomy and independence, but have to navigate an increasingly tight job market. It is important that you think carefully about what types of jobs you might be interested in and how you might want to prepare for those roles, and that you discuss those plans with Vivek so that he can effectively mentor you.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Expectations
text:
Graduate Students
Unlike postdocs, grad students have to balance research and coursework, and as a result have a wide range of responsibilities to manage.

Be organized: Grad school is full of demands on your time and can be stressful. Make sure that you develop a time management system that works to manage your responsibilities, both research and coursework, while allowing sufficient time off to decompress. There is no universal strategy, but identifying how to manage your time is one of the biggest challenges of grad school.
Ask questions: As a grad student, you are learning how to do research, or an equivalent type of professional work for M.Eng. and M.P.S. students. Make sure that you actively ask questions if anything, whether a science question, a research plan, course suggestions, or an administrative issue, is unclear to you.
Develop a research plan: Our research group uses a broad variety of methods to address problems across a number of application domains. As such, there is a large degree of freedom to identify areas which you find exciting, rather than simply working on problems which Vivek assigns you. It is, of course, understood that this plan is likely to be dynamic and may change as you engage in research, are exposed to other areas or ideas in seminars or by talking to collaborators, or take additional courses. The important thing is that you are working on problems which you find fulfilling and intellectually stimulating.
Stay in good standing: Graduate programs have a wide variety of requirements, from required courses and credits to exam dates. While Vivek will help you manage these requirements, it is important that you stay on top of them and your status and communicate with him about any upcoming deadlines or needs.
Focus on your research: If you’re in a thesis-based program (an M.S. or a Ph.D.), your research is the most important part of your graduate education. For students in professional programs (M.Eng. and M.P.S.), your project is a key part of your overall experience. You should prioritize your research as such and treat it professionally.
Succeed in your coursework: Depending on your program, there are periods (or your entire program) in grad school that are dominated by coursework. You should try to get as much from your coursework as possible (while meeting your other responsibilities) and connect it to your research whenever possible.
Develop independence: You should not hesitate to pursue and discuss your own ideas as they arise. Within the context of your time management system (and without compromising your personal time), set aside time to read new papers in and out of your field, attend as many seminars as you can, and run independent experiments with new models and datasets. Make sure you discuss ideas and results with Vivek and the broader group for feedback.
Develop a career plan: There is no hiding the fact that there is a clear opportunity cost to attending graduate school. You should think carefully about what type of job you would like to have, and what credential and what type of training would best prepare you for your ambitions. This plan is likely to be dynamic, and communication with Vivek and others in the group is important.

title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Expectations
text:
Undergraduate Students
Undergrads who are working with the research group have several responsibilities.

Learn!: As an undergrad, you are not necessarily expected to write and publish papers or give presentations (though it’s great for your resume if you can!). However, you should link your research to your broader education and learn as much as you can from the process. This may help you decide if you want to go to graduate school.
Succeed in your coursework: Research activities should be viewed as a supplement to undergrad education, not a primary requirement. As such, your first responsibility is to make sure that you remain in good academic standing and are on track to graduate with a strong GPA.
Work 3 hours each week for every credit hour: This is the standard conversion from credit-hours to work-hours. Both your research and your classwork will have varying demands from week to week, but try to work this many hours each week on average. If you find yourself needing to work more than this to complete your project, let Vivek and anyone else you’re working with know so they can scale the scope back.
Stay on top of deadlines: It is your responsibility to be aware of upcoming deadlines for course content or for paperwork, and make Vivek aware of what he needs to do or how he can help you complete the relevant task(s).

title: AI Tools in Research
text: This page covers how we use language models and related tools in the group’s research, and how to decide when a use isn’t appropriate.

title: AI Tools in Research
text:
Cognitive Offloading
Our concern on this page is with what these tools do to your skills, which is a separate question from whether their output is accurate. Because the tools are useful, it’s easy to hand them work without noticing that you’ve stopped practicing it.
This problem was described long before language models. Bainbridge’s “Ironies of Automation”1 looked at automated process control and flight decks, where operators are left to monitor the automation and take over when something goes wrong. The paper argues that the operator is left with the tasks the designers couldn’t automate, including the take-over, while automation removes the practice those tasks need: manual skills “deteriorate when they are not used,” and the knowledge needed to handle an unusual situation “develops only through use and feedback about its effectiveness.”
1 Bainbridge, L. (1983). Ironies of automation. Automatica, 19(6), 775–779. https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8.2 Liu, G., Christian, B., Dumbalska, T., Bakker, M. A., & Dubey, R. (2026). AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance. Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04721.3 Kosmyna, N., Hauptmann, E., Yuan, Y. T., Situ, J., et al. (2025). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872.Two recent studies find related effects with AI assistants. In a set of randomized experiments with 1,222 online participants solving fraction problems and reading-comprehension questions, people who had AI help did better while they had it, then solved fewer problems and skipped more of them once the help was removed, compared with people who never had it2. These effects appeared after sessions of only 10–15 minutes. In an EEG study of 54 people writing essays over several months, participants who used an LLM showed the weakest neural connectivity of three groups (LLM, search engine, no tools). In a final session, nine of the LLM users wrote without it; they showed weaker connectivity, and 7 of the 9 could not quote a sentence from the essay they had just written, against 1 of the 9 participants who switched the other way3.
These studies are short or small (the crossover result in the essay study rests on 18 people), and the essay study has not been peer reviewed yet, so they do not tell us how large the effect is over years of research. They are consistent with Bainbridge’s mechanism, though, and that mechanism is the reason for the guidance on this page.

title: AI Tools in Research
section: Deciding Whether a Use Is Reasonable
text:
Deciding Whether a Use Is Reasonable
For any use you’re unsure about, ask: could I check this output myself, with the skills I have now?
If you could, the tool is saving you time on work you already know how to do, and you’re still responsible for the result. If you could not, and you would be accepting the output because you cannot evaluate it, then the tool is doing the judgment for you, which is what we want to avoid.
The answer depends on what you know, so the same use can be fine for one person and not for another. Having a model draft boilerplate in a language you know well is fine. Having it write an analysis using a method you don’t understand isn’t, even if the code runs and the numbers look reasonable.

title: AI Tools in Research
AI Tools in Research
text:
The Group’s Skills
The group maintains claude-research-skills (private to the group), a set of Claude Agent Skills built around our workflow: adversarial reading, paper planning, literature review, figure design, code review, and revision response.
The skills review and help plan work that you’re doing; they don’t write it for you. The repository’s design notes put it this way for the paper-planning skill:

What comes out of this conversation is not your contract. It is a draft, with placeholders, the assistant’s compressions of what you said, and suggestions marked as suggestions. The hypothesis, the scope decision, and the framing have to be yours. […] A contract you did not write is a contract you will not maintain, and its entire value is that it records what you predicted before you knew the answer.

The other skills follow the same rule. Referee simulation only works on your own papers, the revision-response skill evaluates a reply you have written instead of writing one, author lists are never filled in by inference, and the literature skill will not name a paper it has not found in a search.
Installation instructions are in the repository README.

title: AI Tools in Research
text:
Reproducibility
Our reproducibility commitments apply to code a model helped write in the same way as to any other code:

You are responsible for all the code in your analysis, including code you did not write yourself. Generated code usually runs, so the syntax errors that would normally warn you something is off are missing, while logic errors can remain.
Test it the way you would test any code. Positive and negative controls are the relevant checks: does it recover known values, and does it find nothing in noise?
Be most careful where the numbers are hardest to check by eye (uncertainty propagation, tail estimates), since a plausible wrong answer there will not stand out.
Internal code review before submission is already required. Tell the reviewer which parts were generated.

title: AI Tools in Research
text:
Journal and Funder Disclosure
AGU, Elsevier, Springer Nature, PNAS and AMS all state that an AI tool cannot be listed as an author. AGU, Elsevier, Springer Nature and AMS give the same reason: authorship requires accountability, which a tool cannot take. Copernicus goes further and says generative AI must not be used for text or interpretation at all. Our own authorship criteria already rule out AI authorship, since they require both a contribution to the research and participation in drafting and revising the paper.
Beyond authorship, most current policies require:

disclosure of substantial AI use, usually in the Methods or an equivalent section (grammar and spelling checks generally do not need declaring);
full author responsibility for everything in the manuscript, including generated parts;
separate, stricter rules for peer review (see below).

Rules for figures differ the most between publishers: some ban AI-generated images and others allow them with disclosure. Check before you make one.






WarningCheck Your Target Journal



These policies change faster than this page will. The table below was checked in September 2026, so treat it as a starting point and confirm against the journal’s current author guidelines when you submit. Add the disclosure statement to the paper checklist for that submission.





Venue
Policy




AGU
Our main venue. No AI authors. Disclose the tool and how it was used in the Methods. LLMs may not be used to review a manuscript.


Elsevier
No AI authors. A separate declaration section before the references. Different rules for different kinds of images.


Copernicus / EGU
Language editing does not need to be declared; generative use does. Allows AI-generated illustrations if the tool is cited.


Springer Nature
No AI authors. Document use in the Methods. AI-generated images are not permitted.


PNAS
No AI authors. Disclose in the Methods or Acknowledgments.


AMS
No AI authors. Disclose the tool and how it was used. Reviewers may not use AI tools.




NSF
NSF has two separate policies that are easy to confuse:

For proposal preparation, disclosure is encouraged but not required. NSF asks proposers to say in the project description whether and how they used generative AI (December 2023 notice).
For research misconduct, PAPPG 24-1 Supplement 1 (effective December 2025) extends the definition to fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism committed “through the use or assistance of other persons, entities, or tools, including artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools.”

The second policy does not add a disclosure requirement, but it does mean a fabricated citation in a proposal is misconduct whether or not a model produced it.

title: AI Tools in Research
text:
Peer Review and Confidentiality






ImportantKeep Manuscripts Under Review Out of AI Tools



A manuscript sent to you for review is confidential, and uploading it to an external service breaks that confidentiality regardless of what the service does with it. AGU, Elsevier, Springer Nature and AMS all tell reviewers not to upload manuscripts to AI tools, and NSF prohibits reviewers from uploading proposal content to tools it has not approved.
AMS gives a second reason: an AI system cannot explain the reasoning behind its evaluation, so the exchange between authors and reviewers that a review is meant to start cannot happen.
If you’re asked to review and would like help, please ask Vivek. Reviewing is a skill like the others on this page, and you build it by doing it.

title: AI Tools in Research
text:
Applicants
People applying to join the group have their own guidance on the graduate, postdoc, and undergraduate pages.
An application is the only evidence we have of what a specific person is interested in and why, so we ask applicants to write it themselves. The guided paper evaluation for graduate applicants allows AI tools, because we discuss it with the applicant afterward.

title: AI Tools in Research
text:
Keeping This Page Current
The tools, the policies, and the evidence are all changing. If something here is out of date, please fix it, and if you find a use that has helped your work and isn’t covered here, bring it to lab meeting. The group is still working out how to use these tools well.

title: Coding Best Practices
text: Here are some best practices to follow when writing code.

title: Coding Best Practices
text:
Use Functions
Use functions instead of copying and pasting code blocks. Every time code is copied, it increases the number of lines that need to be edited if that base code is modified, which in turn increases the potential for bugs. If you find yourself repeating code, it’s more effective to write a function, which can be more directly debugged and edited.

title: Coding Best Practices
text:
Write Good Comments
When writing comments, write about “why,” not “what.” What a particular line of code is doing is pretty straightforward to understand. The logic or goal of a section of code is more important to comment so you or anyone else can put those sections and lines into context

title: Coding Best Practices
text:
Write Unit Tests
Unit tests are a great debugging and software validation tool. The purpose of a unit test is to check that a particular function or set of functions behaves as expected. They consist of a few steps:

Set the environment’s state. Initialize variables to desired values for the test.
Execute the desired function(s).
Compare the output to the expected output given the specified variables.

It’s useful to write a file containing the unit tests and add this to the repository; then others can verify that the code works as it should.

title: Coding Best Practices
text:
Positive/Negative Controls
Real data is messy, and it can be easy to rationalize and find explanations for results, even if they’re erroneous. Make sure that your codes and algorithms work properly by conducting positive and negative control tests. A positive control test shows that code can recover known values, e.g. running your calibration code for a data generated by a statistical model with known parameter values. A negative control test shows that your code doesn’t falsely detect patterns, e.g. running the code on white noise.

title: Coding Best Practices
text:
Write READMEs
Scientific code repositories aren’t always useful for reproduction! This can be because of poorly commented and/or written code or because it isn’t clear how to set up a system to run the code. Your README.mdshould explain the purpose of the code, what the dependencies are, including versions (or, if you’ve shared an environment.yml file or something similar, how to set up the environment), and how to reproduce the published results (or extend them if that’s desirable).

title: Coding Best Practices
text:
Use GitHub
A useful Git commit consists of code required to add a new feature or fix a particular bug. This allows easy restoration of a certain code state with a known set of rolled back changes. For larger-scale code revisions, consider creating a new branch which can then be merged with the main branch once that code is fully verified.

title: Figure Library
text:
The group maintains two small packages of plotting defaults with matching functions, so that group figures share a colorblind-safe palette and readable type without each project setting them up again:
They implement a few recommendations from Figure Design, which explains the reasoning behind them.

title: Figure Library
text:
Getting Started

JuliaPython


using Pkg
Pkg.add(url = "https://github.com/srikrishnan-lab/VizLab.jl")
using VizLab, Plots

lab_theme!()                          # once, at the top of a figure script

p = plot(size = journal_size(:single))
spaghetti!(p, years, ensemble; n = 100)
bandplot!(p, years, q05, q95; label = "5–95% ensemble range")
savefig(p, "figures/fig01_slr.png")


pip install git+https://github.com/srikrishnan-lab/vizlab-py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import vizlab

vizlab.lab_theme()                    # once, at the top of a figure script

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=vizlab.journal_size("single"))
vizlab.spaghetti(ax, years, ensemble, n=100)
vizlab.bandplot(ax, years, q05, q95, label="5-95% ensemble range")
fig.savefig("figures/fig01_slr.png")

title: Figure Library
text:
What the Packages Contain







Function
What it does




lab_theme
Readable fonts, no top/right spines, light y-grid only, colorblind-safe palette


lab_palette(n)
Colorblind-safe categorical colors; warns past about 7


sequential() / diverging()
Colormaps for magnitudes and for data with a meaningful midpoint


bandplot
Shaded uncertainty interval


spaghetti
Subsampled ensemble members


journal_size
Single, one-and-a-half, and double column widths



The palettes are Paul Tol’s bright and muted schemes, which are designed to stay distinguishable for readers with the common forms of color-vision deficiency. They are not distinguishable in grayscale (in the bright scheme, blue and green have almost the same lightness), so if a figure has to work in grayscale, vary the line style or marker as well as the color.
lab_palette warns past about seven categories because beyond that, readers have trouble telling hues apart. Use facets or label the lines directly instead.

title: Figure Library
text:
Three Common Figure Errors
The package docstrings warn about three errors that are easy to miss before publication:

Not saying what an uncertainty band is. A 90% credible interval, a 5–95% ensemble range, and one standard error look identical on the page and mean very different things, so the caption has to say which one is shown.
Using a diverging colormap with limits that aren’t symmetric around the midpoint. If the midpoint of the color scale isn’t the midpoint of interest in the data, the figure suggests a center that isn’t there.
Scaling a figure after creating it. Set the figure size when you create it, because scaling afterwards changes the physical font size, which is one way axis labels end up too small to read in print.

title: Figure Library
text:
Ensemble Spaghetti
spaghetti subsamples members by default, because plotting several thousand translucent lines produces a solid block with no visible structure.
While you are exploring results, plot both the individual members and the summary band, since they show different things. The band shows where most of the probability is; the individual lines show whether the ensemble does something a band hides, such as bimodality, crossing trajectories, or members that behave qualitatively differently. Figure Design makes the same point about representations of uncertainty in general.

title: Figure Library
text:
Archiving






ImportantPin the Package Version



A paper’s figures have to regenerate years after publication. If your figure scripts import a package that keeps changing, they will eventually stop reproducing the published figures, and the archive your availability statement points to will no longer match the paper.
Either pin the version in your project’s Manifest.toml or environment file (which the meta-repository archives anyway), or copy the theme function into the paper’s repository.

title: Figure Library
text:
Makie
Makie.jl is the alternative to Plots.jl, and the better choice when you need interactivity, 3D, or fine control over complex multi-panel layouts. Several group projects already use CairoMakie.
The palettes are plain hex strings, so they work in Makie unchanged:
using CairoMakie, VizLab
set_theme!(palette = (color = VizLab.TOL_BRIGHT,), fontsize = 10)
The helper functions only work with Plots.jl. If you find yourself rewriting them for Makie, please open an issue instead of keeping a private copy; if more than one project needs them, we can add a Makie extension.

title: Figure Library
text:
Adding to the Packages
Additions are welcome, especially for plot types the group makes often. The two packages should keep matching functions, so that switching languages doesn’t mean learning a new set of defaults.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text: This page covers how we structure repositories, and how code and data are archived and cited when a paper is submitted. git and GitHub covers the tools themselves, and Data Management covers where data lives while you are still working.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
Repositories and Research Integrity
Repository structure can feel like housekeeping to deal with once the science is done, but it is part of the evidence for a paper. Our stated commitment is that a paper is not ready for peer review if its data and code are not publicly available and documented. A reader who can’t get from your archive to your figures can’t check your work, so the paper isn’t as transparent as it claims to be, and the group’s position on scientific integrity applies to that as much as to the analysis.
In practice, this means setting up the structure in the first week of a project, when it takes a few minutes, instead of reconstructing it during a revision.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
Model Repositories and Meta-Repositories
We split a project across two kinds of repository, and the most common mistake is putting everything in one.
A model repository holds a model: code that is reusable, that will outlive this paper, and that someone else might run for a different question. Start from model_repo_template.
A meta-repository holds one paper’s analysis: the workflow that takes a model and some data and produces this paper’s figures and numbers. Start from paper-metarepo-template.
The meta-repository doesn’t contain the model. It refers to a released version of the model by its DOI.






TipWhy Keep the Model Separate?



Putting a model inside a paper’s repository causes three problems.
The model becomes hard to reuse: the next project has to either copy it, which creates a second version nobody keeps in sync, or depend on a repository named after an earlier paper.
The paper becomes hard to reproduce: a reader can’t tell which parts of the code are the model and which are this analysis, so they can’t tell what your contribution was.
Both become hard to version: a bug fix in the model turns into a commit in a paper repository that was supposed to stay fixed at submission.


If you’re unsure whether something is a model or an analysis, ask whether the next project would want to use it. If it would, it’s a model.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
Starting a Project
Do this in the first week, before there is anything to lose:

Create the repository from the appropriate template, in the srikrishnan-lab organization and not in your personal account. Work that lives only under a personal account leaves with that person.
Give it a provisional name, and rename it to lastname-etal_year_journal once the paper takes shape. GitHub redirects the old URLs after a rename.
Keep it private for now if you like. It has to be public by submission.
Fill in the README as you go. The template’s README has sections for the abstract, journal reference, code and data references, dependencies, and reproduction steps, and filling them in at the end means reconstructing everything from memory.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
Archiving with Zenodo
GitHub is not an archive. Repositories get renamed, made private, transferred, and deleted, so a bare GitHub URL in a data availability statement will eventually stop working.
Zenodo gives you a DOI and a permanent snapshot. Once you connect it to a repository, every GitHub release is archived automatically:

Sign in to Zenodo with your GitHub account and turn on archiving for the repository (GitHub’s instructions).
Create a release on GitHub. Zenodo archives that snapshot and assigns it a DOI.
Add the DOI badge to the top of the README.







ImportantConcept DOI vs. Version DOI



Zenodo gives you two DOIs, and they point to different things:

the version DOI points to one specific release, which never changes;
the concept DOI points to the record as a whole, and always resolves to the latest version.

Cite the version DOI in a paper. A reader following your data availability statement has to land on the code that produced your results, and the concept DOI will lead them to whatever the code has become since.
Cite the concept DOI for a resource you expect people to keep using while you keep updating it.
If you cite the concept DOI in a paper by mistake, the link keeps working, so nobody notices that it now points to different code than the paper describes.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
Before Submission
Do these steps in order, because each depends on the one before:

Make both repositories (model and meta) public.
Release and archive the model first. The meta-repository has to cite a specific version of the model, and that version doesn’t exist until you’ve created the release.
Archive the input and generated data, including large simulation ensembles and not only the subset the paper used, so that readers can see how the subset was chosen.
Release and archive the meta-repository, with the model and data DOIs already filled in its README.
Write the availability statement using those DOIs instead of URLs.
Ask someone who wasn’t involved to reproduce the analysis from the archive and the README alone, as the paper checklist requires. This is usually how hard-coded absolute paths get caught.

An availability statement should say what is archived, where, and under which DOI. For example:

All code and data required to reproduce this analysis are archived at [DOI]. The [model name] model version used is archived at [DOI]. Input data are available from [source] and archived at [DOI].

Check your target journal’s requirements for this statement, since they vary and some journals require a specific section heading.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
Licensing
Every repository needs a license. Code without one isn’t open, whatever the repository’s visibility: without a license, other people have no legal permission to reuse, modify, or redistribute it, and having it on GitHub doesn’t change that.
Selecting Licenses covers the choice. Use a permissive license (MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0) for original code, and match the upstream license when you build on copyleft code.

title: GitHub and Zenodo
text:
When Someone Leaves
Repository ownership, releases that haven’t been made yet, and who maintains a model after its author graduates are covered in Leaving the Group. Please read it well before you leave, since these questions are much harder to sort out after the person has gone.

title: Using Hopper
text: This page covers how to get onto Hopper, work on it comfortably, and run jobs. The overview covers what Hopper is and when it’s the right tool.

title: Using Hopper
text:
Getting an Account
You log in to Hopper with a CAC account, which is separate from your Cornell NetID. You get one by being added to the group’s CAC project; please message Vivek, since this should be part of onboarding.
Once your account exists:
ssh <your_cac_username>@hopper.cac.cornell.edu
You’ll be asked to set a new password the first time you log in. CAC passwords need at least eight characters drawn from at least three of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, and symbols. They expire every six months, and you can reset them at passwordreset.cac.cornell.edu. Repeated failed logins lock the account for about thirty minutes.






NoteDo I Need the VPN or Two-Factor Authentication?



CAC’s documentation doesn’t say whether either is required. If you’re off campus and SSH hangs, try the Cornell VPN before assuming your account is broken, and ask CAC if the problem continues.

title: Using Hopper
text:
SSH Keys
SSH keys are optional, but please set them up: they remove the password prompt, and remote editors need to log in without one.
On your own machine:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "hopper"          # accept the defaults
ssh-copy-id <your_cac_username>@hopper.cac.cornell.edu
Then add a host block to ~/.ssh/config so you can type ssh hopper:


~/.ssh/config

Host hopper
    HostName hopper.cac.cornell.edu
    User <your_cac_username>
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ServerAliveCountMax 10

ServerAliveInterval stops idle connections from being dropped, which matters for long interactive sessions.
CAC also creates a key pair for you on the cluster itself. That key is for communication between nodes inside jobs (MPI and similar) and is unrelated to the key you use to log in.

title: Using Hopper
text:
Remote Editing
Editing files on Hopper from an editor on your laptop is much easier than editing in a terminal. All three options below use ordinary SSH.






WarningWhere Does My Editor Run Code?



VS Code and JetBrains both install a background server on the machine you connect to, and that server runs as you on the head node. Editing files that way is fine. Pressing Run or Debug in the editor is not, because it runs your analysis on the head node.
Use the editor to edit files and submit jobs. To run something interactively, start an interactive session in a terminal and work inside it.
Language servers and indexing extensions also use the head node’s CPU. If you point a Python or Julia extension at a large repository, it will index the repository on the head node, so keep your extensions to the ones you need. If you’re told you’re loading the head node, check this first.
CAC doesn’t document remote editors. The setups below work because Hopper supports standard SSH, and CAC hasn’t endorsed them.



VS Code
Install the Remote - SSH extension, run “Remote-SSH: Connect to Host”, and pick hopper (it reads the ~/.ssh/config block above). The first time you connect, VS Code installs its server into ~/.vscode-server, which takes a minute or two and uses some of your home-directory space.


JetBrains
JetBrains Gateway connects with the same SSH configuration and installs a full backend IDE under ~/.cache/JetBrains. That takes more space than the VS Code server, so if your home directory is nearly full, use VS Code.


Plain SSH
A terminal session needs nothing beyond SSH:
ssh hopper
tmux new -s work       # or: tmux attach -t work
With tmux, a dropped connection doesn’t end what you were doing. Learn this even if you use an editor, because it’s what you fall back on when the editor’s server won’t start. The shell page has more.

title: Using Hopper
text:
Moving Files
For a few files, use rsync with your SSH configuration:
rsync -avP ./localdir/ hopper:~/remotedir/      # up
rsync -avP hopper:~/remotedir/ ./localdir/      # down
For large transfers, use Globus, which resumes interrupted transfers and checks that files arrived intact. Hopper’s collection is named Hopper Cluster.

title: Using Hopper
text:
Software and Environments

Modules
Hopper uses Lmod:
module avail            # what is installed
module spider <name>    # search, including modules not currently loadable
module load R/4.1.0     # case-sensitive
module list
module purge            # start clean
Load modules inside your job script as well as in your login shell, so the job doesn’t depend on your interactive environment.


Python






WarningCan I Use conda on Hopper?



The conda page describes your own machine. On Hopper, CAC documents only venv and pip, there is no python3 module to load, and the system Python is version 3.6, which is old.
If your work needs a current Python, please talk to Vivek before spending time on this, since the setup from your laptop may not carry over. The options include building a newer Python yourself, using a Singularity container (module load singularity), or installing Miniforge in your home directory.


python3 -m venv ~/envs/myproject
source ~/envs/myproject/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt


R
module load R
mkdir -p $R_LIB
After that, install.packages('<name>') inside R installs packages into your home directory.


Julia
Julia is available as a module, but it may be an older version. Installing juliaup in your home directory lets you choose the version, which you’ll usually want for a project with a committed Manifest.toml.

title: Using Hopper
text:
Running Jobs
Hopper uses Slurm and has two partitions:



Partition
Nodes
Time limit




normal
all
none


guest
all
48 hours









NoteHow Does Slurm Count CPUs?



Hyperthreading is on, so Slurm treats each physical core as two CPUs: -n 1 gives you two logical CPUs, which is one physical core. Add --ntasks-per-core=1 if you want to ignore hyperthreading and count physical cores.



Batch Jobs


job.sh

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J myjob             # job name
#SBATCH -p normal            # partition
#SBATCH -t 04:00:00          # walltime, hh:mm:ss
#SBATCH -n 1                 # tasks
#SBATCH -c 8                 # CPUs per task
#SBATCH -o logs/%x-%j.out    # stdout (%x = name, %j = job id)
#SBATCH -e logs/%x-%j.err    # stderr
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@cornell.edu

module purge
module load gnu9

source ~/envs/myproject/bin/activate
python analysis.py

To submit and monitor it:
mkdir -p logs          # Slurm will not create it, and the job fails if it is missing
sbatch job.sh
squeue -u $USER
scancel <job_id>
scontrol show job <job_id>
Always set -t to a realistic time. The normal partition has no limit, so a job that hangs will hold resources the rest of the cluster needs until someone cancels it.


Interactive Sessions
For debugging, exploratory work, or anything you would otherwise be tempted to run on the head node, start an interactive session:
srun -p normal -n 1 -c 8 --pty /bin/bash -l
This puts you on a compute node, where you can work normally. Type exit when you’re finished, since CAC asks that you release the allocation instead of leaving it idle.
Start the session from inside tmux on the head node, so that a dropped connection doesn’t end it.
CAC documents srun --pty but not salloc. salloc may work, but srun --pty is the documented way.


Job Arrays
Much of the group’s work is an ensemble of independent tasks (Monte Carlo replicates, parameter sweeps, one task per scenario), and a job array is the way to run it:


array.sh

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J ensemble
#SBATCH -p normal
#SBATCH -t 02:00:00
#SBATCH -n 1
#SBATCH -c 4
#SBATCH --array=1-500%50     # 500 members, at most 50 running at once
#SBATCH -o logs/%x-%A_%a.out

module purge
source ~/envs/myproject/bin/activate
python run_member.py --member $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

Keep the %50 limit, because it leaves capacity for the other three groups sharing the cluster. Each task reads its member number from $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; use it to set the random seed, to index into a parameter table, and to name the output file.


Chained and Dependent Jobs
When a workflow has stages (calibrate, then simulate, then post-process), submit them with dependencies so each stage starts when the previous one finishes:
jid1=$(sbatch --parsable calibrate.sh)
jid2=$(sbatch --parsable --dependency=afterok:$jid1 simulate.sh)
sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid2 postprocess.sh
With afterok, a job runs only if the previous job succeeded. To wait for an entire array, use --dependency=afterok:$jid with the array’s job ID; the dependent job starts once every task has finished.


Staging Data Through /tmp
Home directories are on NFS, shared across all nodes, so heavy reading and writing from many tasks at once slows the file system for everyone. CAC says: “We cannot stress enough how important this is to avoid delays on the file systems.”
If your job does heavy file I/O, copy inputs to the node’s local /tmp first, work there, and copy results back at the end:
MYTMP=/tmp/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID
mkdir -p $MYTMP || exit 1
cp -rp $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/inputs $MYTMP/ || exit 1

cd $MYTMP && python analysis.py

cp -rp $MYTMP/output $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/ || exit 1
rm -rf $MYTMP
This is most important for job arrays, where the load grows with the number of tasks running at once.

title: Using Hopper
text:
FAQ

Why is my job stuck in PENDING?
squeue -u $USER shows the reason. Resources means the cluster is busy, which is normal; wait. Priority means other jobs are queued ahead of yours. PartitionTimeLimit means your -t is longer than the partition allows. If a job has been pending for days, please ask before resubmitting it.


Why is my job slower than on my laptop?
There are two common causes. Hopper’s Intel cores run at 2.1 GHz, well below a typical workstation, so serial code really is slower there (see when to use Hopper). Or your job spends its time reading and writing files on NFS, in which case stage the data through /tmp.


How do I get more memory?
The AMD nodes (c0023-c0026) have 567 GB of memory, against 192 GB on the Intel nodes. Request memory with --mem= or --mem-per-cpu=, or ask for the large nodes with -w.


How do I see what a finished job used?
Try sacct -j <job_id> or seff <job_id>. These are standard Slurm tools, but CAC’s documentation doesn’t mention them, so they may not be set up on Hopper. Please try them and tell the rest of us whether they work.


I ran out of space in my home directory. What now?
Check with du -sh ~/*. Editor servers, conda environments, and old job output often take the most space. Remember that nothing on Hopper is backed up; Data Management explains where data should go instead.


Is there a web interface?
No. CAC’s Open OnDemand portal is for the Seneca cluster, and Hopper is reached only through SSH.


Something is broken, and it isn’t my code. Who do I tell?

text:
This section contains guides and team resources for common workflows and tasks.
If you’re new, start with Meetings, Group Workflow (the software we coordinate with), Data Management (where your data should live and what is backed up), GitHub and Zenodo (how projects are structured and archived), and AI Tools in Research.

title: Meetings
text: The group has two standing meetings, both on Monday afternoons in Riley-Robb 319, plus one-on-ones with Vivek. This page covers what each is for and what to bring.

title: Meetings
text:
Lab Meeting
Lab meeting is on Mondays from 1:00 to 2:30pm in Riley-Robb 319. You can also attend remotely; the Zoom link is in the labmeetings repository instead of here, since this manual is public.
Lab meeting is the group’s main shared working session. A typical slot is one person presenting, and a presentation can be any of the following (the most useful ones are often the least polished):

Work in progress, including work that is not going well
A practice talk before a conference or an exam
A figure you are not sure about
A method you are trying to understand, taught to the rest of us
A problem you are stuck on

Asking for help when you’re stuck is an explicit expectation of everyone in the group, and lab meeting is the main place to do it. Having four people who know different things look at the same problem for an hour is often a better use of the time than a polished update.

Preparing
Add your item to the current meeting’s agenda file in labmeetings before the meeting. How much you prepare depends on the slot: a practice talk needs to be ready, while a problem you’re stuck on only needs a clear statement of the problem and what you’ve already tried.
You don’t need slides. A figure on the screen and a conversation often work better.


Attending
Attendance is expected, in person or remotely, as part of maintaining a presence in the group. If you can’t make it, please say so in Slack beforehand.
Come having thought about other people’s work as well as your own. The group’s internal peer review and code review before submission depend on people knowing enough about each other’s projects to be useful readers, and lab meeting is where most of that knowledge comes from.

title: Meetings
text:
Journal Club
Journal club is on Mondays from 2:30 to 3:30pm in Riley-Robb 319, directly after lab meeting.
One person presents one paper each week. The presenter picks the paper, which doesn’t have to be new or something you already understand. Papers you found hard, or that you disagree with, often lead to a better discussion than papers you can summarize cleanly.
The reading list is a reasonable source of candidates, particularly the foundational papers everyone in the group is expected to have read.

Claiming a Slot
Open a pull request against the schedule table in journal-club adding your name and the paper (with a link) to an open date. Doing this a week or two ahead gives people time to read it.


Presenting
Read the paper closely and skim its main references. You aren’t expected to defend the paper or to have resolved every question about it. Your job is to help everyone else understand it quickly and then lead a discussion: fifteen or twenty minutes of setup and forty minutes of discussion is a better split than the reverse.
It is completely acceptable, and often the most interesting outcome, to present a paper and conclude that you do not believe its central claim.

title: Meetings
text:
One-on-Ones with Vivek
Weekly, scheduled for an hour, arranged at the start of each semester around everyone’s teaching and coursework.
An hour is what gets reserved, not what has to be used. Plenty of weeks need twenty minutes, and ending early is a perfectly good outcome: the hour exists so that the weeks which do need it are not squeezed. The purpose is to update each other and to talk through anything that is proving difficult, not to fill the time.
These meetings are yours. Vivek will not arrive with an agenda unless something specific needs discussing, so bring one (even a rough one). Useful things to bring:

Where things stand since last time, and anything you are stuck on
A decision you need input on
Results you want a second opinion about, before they harden into a paper
Coursework, committee, exam, and deadline logistics
Career questions, which are in scope and do not need a special occasion







ImportantDo I Need to Make Progress Every Week?



Do not treat the meeting as a weekly accounting of output. Expecting substantial progress every single week is unrealistic, and measuring yourself that way is a reliable route to feeling like you are failing at a job you are doing fine.
Research does not arrive on a seven-day cycle. A week can go to a bug that turns out to be a one-character fix, to a method that does not work, to reading that does not resolve into anything yet, or to coursework. None of that is wasted: it is what the work consists of, and it is often where the understanding comes from.
So the honest report is the useful one. “This didn’t work and I’m not sure why” is a better agenda item than a polished summary, because it is the kind of thing the meeting can actually help with. The meeting is more valuable when it is accurate than when it is impressive.


If something urgent comes up between meetings, don’t wait for the next one. PI availability explains how to reach Vivek.

title: Paper Writing
text: Paper writing is essential for M.S. and Ph.D students as well as postdocs. While it is less so for undergrads, M.Eng., and M.P.S. students, turning your project into a paper could have benefits down the road.

title: Paper Writing
text:
Process Guidelines

Start with an outline and paper contract. This will help lay out the goals of the research and make sure all projected authors know their expected contributions and how key terms are being used (as vocabularies can vary across disciplines or even sub-disciplines – the Glossary records how this group uses the ambiguous ones).
In our group, the first author (usually the junior researcher leading the research) has the final say on scope, wording, and figure design. These decisions should be made in consultation with the entire team, however.
Don’t expect immediate turnaround when submitting drafts for feedback, either to Vivek or to the other authors! Depending on how busy Vivek is, he might take up to a week to provide feedback, though doing so in a timely fashion will always be a top priority. Other authors may take a longer time depending on their constraints. This is especially important to bear in mind when revising a paper.
Our group’s best practice is to do internal peer review before submitting a paper. After focusing on a piece of research, it is easy to believe that certain concepts can be taken as given or are implicit, which may limit the accessibility of the writing and complicate peer review. To reduce this risk, we will ask two or three group members who were not involved in the project to read the manuscript and provide feedback. If appropriate group members are not available, we will seek out external collaborators for this role. Anyone who provides feedback should be listed in the Acknowledgements section.
Similarly, our group’s best practice is to do an internal code review before submitting a paper. We want our work to be reproducible and to ensure that there are no bugs driving the results, so code should be accessible, well-documented, and presented with a clear workflow. We will ask one member of the group to reproduce the workflow to make sure that the results and figures are reproducible. Anyone who helps with code reviewing should be listed in the Acknowledgements section.

title: Paper Writing
text:
Other Guidelines
Aim to always follow the American Geophysical Union’s author guidelines when writing, whether or not submitting to an AGU journal:

Present a precise and accurate account of the research performed and a clear, objective discussion of its significance.
Include sufficient detail and reference to sources of information in a manuscript to permit the author’s peers to repeat the work.1
Identify sources of all information and cite those publications that have been influential in determining the nature of the reported work and that guide the reader quickly to the primary and other earlier work essential for understanding the present investigation. Information obtained privately, as in conversation or correspondence, should not be used or reported without explicit permission from the source.
Carefully document methodology, assumptions, and uncertainty.2
Follow the appropriate procedures in force in their countries that govern the ethics of work done with human or animal subjects.3
Never plagiarize the work or ideas of others or your own work. Always provide appropriate citation. [The AGU provides additional guidelines on plagiarism at the same link.]
Avoid unnecessary fragmentation or redundant publication of research reports to artificially increase the number of publications.4
Never include personal criticism in a written piece of work.5
Report to the editor any changes made to the manuscript after acceptance.
Include as coauthors only those persons who have made significant scientific contributions to the work and determine order of authorship in a manner appropriate to the contribution. All coauthors share responsibility for the quality and integrity of the submitted and published manuscript.
Reveal to the editor any potential conflict of interest for any author that might be affected by publication of the results contained in a manuscript or in the development of the research.
List all funding sources and sources of data or other in-kind support for all authors in the acknowledgments.
In the role of corresponding author, ensure that all coauthors are fully cognizant of the steps and changes in the manuscript during the peer review process.

1 Make sure that you also provide links to the code and data repositories.2 Documenting and characterizing uncertainty is difficult, but it is a key part of all of our analyses. We should be transparent about assumptions and honest about limitations. Good practice is to examine the impact of assumptions when possible, but they and how they might limit the generalizability of the analysis must be made clear in the paper.3 We do not often work with human subjects, but be familiar with these procedures before beginning any project that involves them.4 This is along the idea of “minimal publishable units.” Papers should clearly and thoroughly address 1-3 key questions and contain the same number of key points.5 Always be constructive when reviewing or engaging with other people’s work. Other papers aren’t “flawed” or “contain gaps,” but they might leave open questions due to the assumptions or methods that you are now addressing. Science builds off other work, and we all have to make choices when designing a particular piece of research.

title: Paper Writing
text:
Selecting Journals
Selecting journals for submission is a key part of the paper writing process. This should be done early on, as different journals have difference emphases and audiences, which can greatly impact writing style.
You should select 4-5 journals that you would like to submit to. These can range in terms of ambition and technical emphases — for example, Nature is highly prestigious but more general, while the Journal of Flood Risk Management is a solid journal with a more specific and technical focus. Ask yourself the following questions (Vivek will help!):

What is the key question and hypothesized point of the paper? Is it a question that might get the attention of a more general audience, or is it addressing a more technical issue that specialists would be more interested in?
How well does the scope of the journal align with your key question? Have they published related work?
What are the word and figure limits of the journal and anticipated submission type? Tighter word limits can be difficult for more complex or technical analyses.
How much time do you want to invest in revisions and (if the paper is rejected) in reformatting/reframing the paper for a different journal? More selective journals can have a higher career payoff (though some of the more technical journals publish work that is at least as good and will generate citations over time) but have a higher probability of rejection.
How often have you published a paper in the journal? Over-publishing in the same journal can look strange, particularly if it isn’t one of the top journals.

Based on these considerations, come up with your journal submission sequence. You can sort these journals along various lines, including impact factor (as a proxy for ambition) or similarity of formatting (for example, going from Nature to Nature Climate Change instead of going from Nature to PNAS and then Nature Climate Change).

title: Paper Writing
text:
Paper Contract
Writing a paper contract early in the research design facilitates conversations about authorship, author contributions, research scope, and submission plans. This document should include:

Author line
Expected author contributions
Key research questions
Research hypotheses
Key prior work to address
Methods (broadly speaking)
Submission plan

title: Paper Writing
text:
Outline
Papers should be organized using an outline. How you incorporate this outline into the writing process is up to you: Vivek prefers to expand the outline to full detail, then convert items to sentences and paragraphs, but you might prefer to switch to sentences earlier. However, an outline provides an organized way to facilitate feedback, and we should converge on it before advancing in the writing process.
Outlines are dynamic documents and will evolve over the course of the research, as key questions and findings and methods change. They should be broadly organized as follows (though some of the sections may be in a different order depending on the targeted journal’s requirements):

Projected title
Projected author line
Targeted journal
Key research questions
Hypothesized key points (which will be replaced by key findings once these are available)
Abstract
Introduction (including literature review)
Methods
Results
Caveats
Discussion & Conclusions
Acknowledgements
Author contribution statements

title: Letters of Recommendation
Glossary
text: We work across climate science, statistics, decision analysis, and engineering, and those fields use some of the same words differently. This page records how the group uses them. When you settle terminology with coauthors in a paper contract, start here.

title: Glossary
text:
Kinds of Uncertainty

Deep uncertainty

The situation where the parties to a decision don’t know, or can’t agree on, the system model, the probability distributions of its inputs, or how to value the outcomes. It is different from a large amount of ordinary uncertainty: you can’t write down an agreed probability distribution, which is why expected-value methods are no longer the obvious tool. The term also names a research community, decision-making under deep uncertainty.

Parametric uncertainty

Uncertainty about the values of a model’s parameters, with its structure held fixed. Most analyses propagate this kind, because a Monte Carlo ensemble over a fixed model captures it.

Structural uncertainty

Uncertainty about the form of the model itself: which processes are represented, how they are coupled, and what is left out. Two group studies on the reading list found it larger than parametric uncertainty in the systems they examined, so that analyses propagating only parametric uncertainty understated risk, often in the tail.

Model discrepancy

The systematic difference between a model’s output and the system it represents, beyond observation error. It is a property of the model’s structure, not random noise.








WarningHow Is Discrepancy Different From a Residual?



A residual is what is left over after fitting a model to data. Discrepancy is the claim that the model is wrong in a structured way. The difference has consequences for calibration: if you ignore discrepancy, the fitted parameters absorb the structural error, so their estimates tend to be biased and their uncertainty intervals too narrow.
Our own materials have not always kept the two apart, and the reading list includes Brynjarsdóttir and O’Hagan for this reason. Use “discrepancy” when you mean the structural difference.



Epistemic and aleatory uncertainty

Epistemic uncertainty comes from lack of knowledge and can in principle be reduced by learning more; aleatory uncertainty is variability in the system itself, which can’t. Where the boundary falls depends on the model and is often arguable, so treat the distinction as a modeling choice.

title: Glossary
text:
Risk

Risk

Commonly broken into hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, which interact instead of simply multiplying. Which of the three contributes the most uncertainty depends on the analysis. Hosseini-Shakib et al. (2024, on the reading list) found projected riverine flood risk most sensitive to hazard factors, while other group work has found that uncertainty in how buildings are described and valued can be large enough to change which management option looks best.

Hazard

The physical event and its characteristics over space and time: the flood, the storm surge, the heat wave.

Exposure

What is in harm’s way: assets, people, infrastructure.

Vulnerability

How much damage exposed assets take for a given hazard. Depth-damage functions are the standard example.








NoteTwo Uses of “Hazard”



In careful use, hazard is one of the three parts of risk. In looser use, including in some of our own older papers, it stands for the whole risk estimate. Check which meaning a paper intends before assuming the narrow one.

title: Glossary
text:
Models and Their Evaluation

Exploratory modeling

Using ensembles of plausible models to map what could happen and which possibilities matter, instead of treating one model as a stand-in for the system and asking what will happen. The alternative is called consolidative modeling. Exploratory modeling is the group’s basic epistemic stance, and Bankes is the reading-list entry that explains it.

Emulator

A fast statistical approximation of an expensive model (also called a surrogate), fitted to a sample of the model’s runs. Emulators are used when the full model is too slow for the number of evaluations an analysis needs.

Sensitivity analysis

Attributing the variation in a model’s output to variation in its inputs. Global sensitivity analysis varies inputs across their full ranges at the same time; local analysis perturbs them around one point. For nonlinear models with interactions, which describes many of ours, local results can be badly misleading. The MSD uncertainty eBook is the group’s practical reference.

Calibration

Estimating model parameters from observations.








WarningTwo Senses of Verification and Validation



In the modeling sense, Oreskes et al. (on the reading list) argue that verification and validation of numerical models of natural systems are impossible, because natural systems are never closed and model results are never unique. In their words, models “can be confirmed by the demonstration of agreement between observation and prediction, but confirmation is inherently partial,” and they “can only be evaluated in relative terms.”
In the software sense used in Coding Best Practices, “validation” means unit testing and “verified” means reviewed and merged.
Both senses appear in this manual. Check which one is meant, and make it clear when you write.

title: Glossary
text:
Projections and Scenarios

Projection

A conditional statement of what the model says follows given a scenario. It is not a forecast, because it holds only under the scenario’s assumptions.

Prediction

An unconditional claim about what will happen. We rarely make them.

Scenario

A coherent, internally consistent description of a possible future, used as an input assumption. A scenario is not a probability statement, and SSPs and RCPs are not ranked by likelihood.

State of the world (SOW)

One fully specified combination of uncertain factors, and the unit of a large ensemble. An analysis over tens of thousands of SOWs asks which combinations produce outcomes we care about, not which combination is most likely.

title: Glossary
text:
Decision-Making

Robustness

How well a strategy performs across a wide range of futures, as opposed to how well it performs in expectation. Robust strategies usually give up some performance in the most likely future to avoid failing badly in others.

Resilience

The capacity of a system to absorb a disturbance and recover its function. Resilience is a property of the system; robustness is a property of a strategy.

Reliability

In our energy systems work, the technical sense: the probability that a system meets demand under specified conditions.

Regret

The difference between a strategy’s outcome and the best outcome that could have been achieved if the future had been known. Minimizing the maximum regret is one decision criterion under deep uncertainty. The ordinary English word also appears in our writing, so check which is meant.

Rival framings

The observation that how a decision problem is formulated (which objectives, which constraints, whose outcomes count) shapes the answer as much as the analysis does, and that comparing formulations is itself informative.

title: Glossary
text:
Extremes

Return level

The value expected to be exceeded once, on average, over a given period. The 100-year return level is the flood level exceeded on average once per century.

Return period

The inverse: the average time between exceedances. “The 100-year flood” is often read as a flood that happens once a century, which is wrong in two ways: the 100 years is a long-run average, and under nonstationarity the underlying distribution itself changes over time.

Block maxima and peaks over threshold

The two standard approaches to extreme value analysis, which fit either the maximum in each block of time (usually a year) or every exceedance above a threshold. The second uses more of the data, but its results can depend strongly on the threshold chosen.

title: Glossary
text:
Group Tools and Conventions

Meta-repository

A repository holding one paper’s analysis, which points to released versions of the models and data it uses instead of containing them. See git and GitHub.

Paper contract

A document agreed early in a project that records the author line, expected contributions, research questions, hypotheses, and submission plan. See Paper Writing.

BRICK

Building blocks for Relevant Ice and Climate Knowledge, a semi-empirical sea-level model used across the group’s coastal work and implemented in the Mimi framework as MimiBRICK.jl.

UNSAFE

UNcertain Structure And Fragility Ensemble, the group’s framework for estimating property-level flood risk under uncertainty in exposure and vulnerability.

MSD

MultiSector Dynamics, the research program studying how human and Earth systems evolve together across sectors. Much of the group’s uncertainty work is part of this community.

title: R
text: R is a statistical programming language, and is highly optimized for that purpose (though additional functionality exists). It can be relatively slow and doesn’t use memory particularly effectively, but it has a wide variety of data analysis and statistical modeling functions and libraries. R syntax is a bit different than other languages, but you may collaborate with people who prefer to work in R, so it’s good to know your way around it.

title: R
text:
Installation
Use the latest version of R that you can, but it’s not essential (usually) to stay on top of updates. R can be managed using conda, but conda only packages a subset of CRAN. It’s still generally good practice to create new environments for different projects.
For project-level reproducibility in R, renv is the standard tool: it records the exact package versions a project uses in an renv.lock file that you commit alongside the code. Use it for anything that will end up in a paper.

title: R
text:
Usage
Hadley Wickham has several good (and freely available online!) R books, depending on your level of familiarity:

R for Data Science (2nd edition)
Advanced R

Kieran Healy has an excellent book on data visualization using the ggplot2 library, which pairs well with our figure design guide.

title: R
text:
Development Environments
RStudio is the best graphical R IDE around. It is developed by Posit (the company formerly called RStudio), and it is still free and open-source.
If you would rather stay in one editor across languages, VS Code has a usable R extension, though RStudio remains the better experience for R-heavy work.

title: git and GitHub
text:
git is a software version control system. git is useful for tracking changes to code, including systematic approaches to adding new features or changing functionality. We use git to track and save code as we’re working on it.
GitHub is one of several online repositories for sharing code (and is commonly used as a remote repository for git). We use GitHub to facilitate collaboration and share code for papers and other projects.

title: git and GitHub
text:
Setting Up Project Repositories

Meta-Repositories






WarningRepository Visibility



It may be prudent to set up initial repositories as private until you’re ready to release the code (which should always be done ahead of paper submission).


When you start a new project, you should create a GitHub meta-repository right away. You can do this in your personal account or as part of the srikrishnan-lab organization. Make sure that your repository name is informative; we will eventually rename this to align with a paper (something like lead_author-etal-year).
A meta-repository is a repository which creates a single point of access for all resources needed to create a published work. We use meta-repositories to avoid mixing data, models, and analysis codes, which can inhibit reproducibility, make the repository cluttered, and make it difficult to re-use models for subsequent projects. You can fork our meta-repository template as a starting point. There is a companion model repository template for model codes, which live in their own repository rather than inside the meta-repository. GitHub and Zenodo explains why we keep them separate and how both are archived before submission.


Repository Guidelines
Some guidelines on how to structure your meta-repository:

Model codes and data should be minted and archived somewhere like Zenodo (this can be set up to occur automatically upon a GitHub release).

You can link to external models and data, particularly if they have a DOI and/or a version number.
If you developed a model for your project, keep it in its own repository and release a specific version for a paper. Link this from the meta-repository README.
Generated data should be archived.

If you generated a unique dataset for your project, the code for this should be included as part of the meta-repository for the paper.
If you’re generating data which will be reused for other projects, it’s worth making a repository just for the generation code and linking to a released version of that repository in the meta-repository.


Avoid hard-coding absolute paths. If you use an external model or data, let the user set a path to point to where they’ve installed those resources, then use paths relative to them in the rest of the code.
Make separate folders for different parts of the analysis to improve readability (e.g. separate data pre-processing, experiment, and figure-generation codes).
Make individual scripts for each figure you are generating. If all of your figures require large files to generate (for example, the results of a large-scale simulation), make another script which loads the data and then calls the figure-generating scripts in turn. Remember, the goal is readability!

title: git and GitHub
text:
Commits
Commits are how you register a particular code state with git. You can see the status of a repository (what files are untracked and which are changed) using git status. From the terminal, you can make commits with


Making Commits

1git add <files to commit>
git commit -m <commit message>


1

This adds the files you would like to associate with a given commit. This does not have to be all of the files you’ve changed if you’ve made multiple changes that you would like to split across multiple commits.


In general, good commit guidance is:

Make commits as often as possible.
Make sure your commit messages are informative. You should be able to tell what changes you made so you can revert if necessary.

title: git and GitHub
text:
Alternatives
There are several alternatives to GitHub, including Bitbucket. You may use whichever online repository you prefer, though we use GitHub for lab-wide management, such as the website and lab manual.
